title: The Financial Services Industry + Bank of England
topic: The Financial Services Industry + Bank of England
summary: How the UK financial services industry works, why intermediaries exist, Bank of England roles, money flows, retail vs wholesale banking, credit unions, and proprietary vs mutual ownership.
examFocus: Which institution type? Why does this intermediary exist? BoE Lender of Last Resort? Which funding model is most risky? FSCS protection limits?
keyPoints: Financial services allow money to act as a medium of exchange and store of value.
Intermediation = money flows through a bank (middleman). Disintermediation = money flows directly (e.g., P2P lending).
P2P lending does NOT have FSCS protection — investors can lose everything.
Bank of England has 5 roles: Monetary Policy, Lender of Last Resort, Financial Stability, Resolution, Issuing banknotes.
MPC sets interest rates to keep CPI inflation at 2%.
Retail deposits are more stable; wholesale funding is more risky (can disappear in a crisis).
Credit unions require a common bond; savings protected by FSCS up to £85,000.
Mutual/building societies are owned by members, not shareholders.
mustMemories: BoE 5 roles: Monetary Policy, Lender of Last Resort, Financial Stability, Resolution, Issuing banknotes.
FSCS deposit limit: £85,000 per depositor per institution.
Wholesale funding is more risky than retail deposits.
examTraps: P2P lending has NO FSCS protection.
FCA and PRA regulate financial advisers — NOT the BoE directly.
BoE is sole issuer of banknotes in England and Wales only.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a role of the Bank of England?
opts: Setting the Bank Rate through the MPC
mcqs.ex: The FCA and PRA regulate financial advisers. The BoE sets monetary policy and is Lender of Last Resort.

mcqs.q: P2P lending is protected by which compensation scheme?
opts: Neither — P2P lending is not protected by either
mcqs.ex: P2P lending is NOT protected by FSCS. Investors can lose their entire investment.

title: Financial Products
summary: All major financial products: deposit accounts, ISAs, gilts, bonds, equities, ETFs, life assurance, critical illness cover, income protection, and how each product fits into a financial plan.
examFocus: Which product solves this client need? What are the key features and risks of each product? How do tax wrappers (ISAs, pensions) affect returns?
keyPoints: Instant access accounts: low interest, high liquidity. High-interest accounts: require minimum balance or notice period.
Personal Savings Allowance: £1,000 (basic rate), £500 (higher rate), £0 (additional rate).
ISA annual allowance: £20,000. JISA: £9,000. LISA: £4,000/year with 25% government bonus (max £1,000 free per year).
LISA is for ages 18–39; for first home (up to £450k) or retirement.
Gilts: government bonds, CGT exempt, index-linked gilts rise with CPI.
Corporate bonds: investment grade (low risk) vs high yield/junk (higher risk).
Convertible bonds can be converted into shares; pay lower interest.
Decreasing term assurance = repayment mortgage. Level term = interest-only mortgage.
CIC pays lump sum on diagnosis of specified illness — NOT the same as life assurance.
Income Protection Insurance (IPI): pays 60–70% of earnings monthly; deferred period 4 weeks to 1 year.
mustMemories: Decreasing term = repayment mortgage. Level term = interest-only mortgage.
CIC = lump sum on diagnosis (not death).
IPI = 60–70% of earnings monthly until return to work, retirement, or policy end.
examTraps: Decreasing term and level term are frequently confused — match to mortgage type.
CIC is NOT life assurance — it pays on diagnosis, not death.
ISA allowance is total across all ISA types, not per type.

mcqs.q: A client has a repayment mortgage of £200,000. Which type of life assurance is most appropriate?
mcqs.ex: Decreasing term assurance matches the reducing mortgage balance of a repayment mortgage.

mcqs.q: What is the LISA government bonus?
mcqs.ex: The government adds a 25% bonus on contributions up to £4,000 per year = £1,000 free money per year.

title: UK Tax Foundations
summary: Income Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Inheritance Tax, Stamp Duty Land Tax, and National Insurance. Core UK taxes that affect every financial planning recommendation.
examFocus: Tax rates, bands, allowances, exemptions, and how financial products interact with these taxes. MRT1/2 loves tax-adjusted return calculations.
keyPoints: Income Tax (2024/25): Personal Allowance £12,570 (0%); Basic rate 20% up to £50,270; Higher rate 40% up to £125,140; Additional rate 45% above £125,140.
Personal Allowance tapers at £100,000: reduces by £1 for every £2 above £100,000; fully removed above £125,140.
CGT Annual Exempt Amount: £3,000 (2024/25). Residential property: 18%/24%. Other assets: 10%/20%.
PPR exemption: main home is generally exempt from CGT.
IHT: 40% on estate above nil-rate band (£325,000). RNRB: additional £175,000 if home passed to direct descendants.
Total IHT-free potential: £500,000 (single) or £1,000,000 (married couple).
IHT taper relief: gifts 3–7 years before death — reduces but does not eliminate IHT.
SDLT: second property adds 3% surcharge on top of standard rates.
First-time buyer SDLT relief: 0% up to £425,000; 5% on £425,001–£625,000.
NI: 35 qualifying years needed for full new State Pension. State Pension age: 66 (rising to 67 by 2028).
mustMemories: SDLT second property: +3% surcharge on top of standard rates.
Full State Pension: 35 years NI contributions.
examTraps: CGT is charged on the gain, not the sale price.
Different CGT rates apply to residential property vs other assets.
Taper relief reduces IHT — it does NOT eliminate it.
SDLT 3% surcharge for second properties is ON TOP OF standard rates, not instead of.

mcqs.q: What is the current personal allowance for income tax (2024/25)?
A client buys a second property for £300,000. What SDLT rate applies to the portion between £250,001–£300,000?
mcqs.ex: The 3% SDLT surcharge for second properties applies on top of standard SDLT rates. The standard 5% rate plus 3% surcharge = 8% on that band.

mcqs.q: How many years of NI contributions are required for the full new State Pension?
mcqs.ex: 35 years of qualifying NI contributions are required for the full new State Pension.

title: Monetary Policy, Inflation and Economic Policy
topic: Monetary Policy, Inflation and Economic Policy
summary: The MPC, inflation targeting, interest rate mechanisms, CPI vs RPI, deflation, and how monetary and fiscal policy affect the economy and mortgage advice.
examFocus: MPC meets 8 times/year, CPI target 2%, what happens when inflation breaches the target corridor, and how rate changes affect tracker vs fixed-rate mortgage holders.
keyPoints: Government economic aims: price stability (CPI 2%), low unemployment, neutral balance of payments, satisfactory growth.
MPC is a sub-committee of the Bank of England that sets the official Bank Rate.
CPI inflation target: 2%. Target corridor: 1%–3%. If breached, Governor must write open letter to Chancellor.
MPC meets 8 times per year (approximately every 6 weeks) — NOT 12.
CPI: government's primary inflation measure, based on 180,000+ price quotes monthly.
RPI: generally higher than CPI, still used as an index but not strictly targeted.
RPIX: RPI excluding mortgage interest payments.
Deflation = general decline in prices (serious risk to economy). Disinflation = slowing rate of price increases (NOT the same as deflation).
Tracker mortgages: immediately affected by BoE rate changes. Fixed-rate mortgages: insulated during the deal period.
Monetary policy (BoE, interest rates) vs Fiscal policy (government, taxation and spending).
mustMemories: CPI target: 2% (Governor writes open letter if above 3% or below 1%).
Tracker mortgages: immediate rate change effect. Fixed-rate: insulated during deal period.
Deflation = prices falling. Disinflation = rate of price increases slowing (NOT falling prices).
Monetary policy = BoE (interest rates). Fiscal policy = Government (tax and spending).
examTraps: MPC meets 8 times per year — NOT monthly (12 times).
Disinflation is NOT the same as deflation.
Fixed-rate mortgage holders are NOT immediately affected when the BoE changes rates.

mcqs.q: The MPC meets how many times per year?
mcqs.ex: The MPC meets 8 times per year, approximately every 6 weeks.

mcqs.q: If CPI inflation falls below 1%, what must the Governor of the BoE do?
opts: Immediately cut interest rates to zero
Write an open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what action is being taken
Inform the Treasury Select Committee only
mcqs.ex: If inflation deviates more than 1% from the 2% target (i.e., above 3% or below 1%), the Governor must write an open letter to the Chancellor.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between deflation and disinflation?
opts: Deflation = prices falling; Disinflation = rate of price increases slowing
Disinflation = prices falling; Deflation = rate slowing
mcqs.ex: Deflation is a general decline in prices. Disinflation is when the price level is still rising but at a slower rate.
